questions.question_text:
A football league has $9000$ registered players split across four age divisions of different sizes.
To survey $300$ players it takes from each division a number of players equal to that division’s share of all registrations.
Which sampling method is described?

options.text: Stratified sampling
Systematic sampling
options.why: Assumes any organised method uses an ordered list and a fixed step of every $k$th player.

options.text: Simple random sampling
options.why: Overlooks that the divisions fix in advance how many players come from each group.

options.text: Self-selected sampling
options.why: Assumes players chose to take part, when the league selected them from its own records.

questions.solution_text:
The population is split into subgroups, and each subgroup supplies players in proportion to its size.
**Stratified sampling**.

questions.question_text:
A radio station invites listeners to phone in and say whether the speed limit on a highway should be lowered, then reports the views of the $640$ listeners who called.
Which statement correctly names and explains the sampling method?

options.text: A self-selected sample, because each listener decided whether to call
A simple random sample, because the station had no control over who called
options.why: Treats a lack of control as randomness, when random selection must be made from the whole population.

options.text: A systematic sample, because the calls were answered in the order received
options.why: Confuses the order calls arrive in with taking every $k$th member of a population list.

options.text: A stratified sample, because callers came from many parts of the highway
options.why: Calls a mixture of callers strata, when no subgroups were defined and members were not chosen at random within each subgroup.

questions.solution_text:
The station selected nobody; each listener decided personally whether to call, so the sample is made up of whoever chose to answer.
**A self-selected sample, because each listener decided whether to call**.

questions.question_text:
A bakery chain has an ordered production list of $3600$ loaves and wants a systematic sample of $45$ loaves.
Which loaves should be taken?

options.text: Every $80$th loaf, after a random start
Every $45$th loaf, after a random start
options.why: Uses the sample size as the step instead of dividing the population by the sample size.

options.text: Every $8$th loaf, after a random start
options.why: Slips a place value when dividing $3600$ by $45$.

options.text: Every $75$th loaf, after a random start
options.why: Divides $3600$ by $48$ rather than by the stated sample size of $45$.

questions.question_text:
A college will take a proportional stratified sample of $120$ of its $3600$ students, using the campuses below.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Campus}&\textbf{Students}\\ \hline \text{City}&1800\\ \text{North}&1200\\ \text{Coast}&600\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&3600\end{array}$
How many Coast students should be in the sample?

options.why: Splits the sample equally between the three campuses instead of using their sizes.
Gives the City campus figure, taken from the largest row rather than the Coast row.
Calculates $600\div100=6$, instead of using the Coast share $\frac{600}{3600}$ and multiplying by the sample size $120$.

questions.solution_text:
Coast students make up $\frac{600}{3600}$ of the college.
$\frac{600}{3600}\times 120$
$=\frac{1}{6}\times 120$
$=20$
**$20$ Coast students**.

questions.question_text:
A courier company will take a proportional stratified sample of $80$ of its $1200$ drivers, using the depots below.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Depot}&\textbf{Drivers}\\ \hline \text{Ashford}&360\\ \text{Belmont}&540\\ \text{Carden}&240\\ \text{Dunley}&60\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&1200\end{array}$
How many drivers should be taken from Ashford, Belmont, Carden and Dunley?

options.why: Takes equal numbers from each depot rather than numbers proportional to depot size.
Uses a sampling fraction of one tenth instead of the $80$ out of $1200$ actually required.
Assigns the correct four numbers to the depots in the reverse of their listed order.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{80}{1200}=\frac{1}{15}$, so each depot supplies $\frac{1}{15}$ of its drivers.
Ashford: $\frac{360}{15}=24$
Belmont: $\frac{540}{15}=36$
Carden: $\frac{240}{15}=16$
Dunley: $\frac{60}{15}=4$
$24+36+16+4=80$
**$24$, $36$, $16$ and $4$ drivers**.

questions.question_text:
A national park wants a proportional stratified sample of $120$ of the $12\,000$ visitors who entered last month, so that the sample reflects all of last month's visitors.
It plans to take $30$ visitors from each of its four entry gates.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Entry gate}&\textbf{Visitors}\\ \hline \text{North}&6400\\ \text{South}&3200\\ \text{East}&1600\\ \text{West}&800\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&12\,000\end{array}$
What is wrong with this plan?

options.text: The gates differ in size, so the sample should be $64$, $32$, $16$ and $8$
The gates differ in size, so the sample should be $53$, $27$, $13$ and $7$
options.why: Turns each gate's share into a percentage and surveys that many visitors, so the four numbers add to $100$ instead of $120$.

options.text: The sample of $120$ is too small, so it should be raised to $480$
options.why: Blames the sample size when the fault is how the sample is divided among the gates.

options.text: Entry gate is the wrong variable, so visitors should be split by age instead
options.why: Changing to age does not correct the unequal sampling shares at the four gates. The plan is meant to reflect the visitors recorded at those gates.

questions.solution_text:
A proportional stratified sample takes from each subgroup in proportion to its size, but the four gates recorded very different numbers of visitors.
$\frac{120}{12\,000}=\frac{1}{100}$, so each gate supplies $\frac{1}{100}$ of its visitors.
North: $\frac{6400}{100}=64$; South: $\frac{3200}{100}=32$; East: $\frac{1600}{100}=16$; West: $\frac{800}{100}=8$
$64+32+16+8=120$
**The gates differ in size, so the sample should be $64$, $32$, $16$ and $8$**.

questions.question_text:
A phone-repair chain tests $3$ of the $900$ replacement screens it received in a delivery, finds no fault in any of them, and reports that the delivery is free of faults.
What is the main weakness of this study?

options.text: Three screens are far too few to show how common a fault is in $900$
The screens should have been chosen by the supplier rather than the chain
options.why: Hands selection to the party with an interest in a clean result, which weakens the study further.

options.text: Testing screens destroys them, so no screen should have been tested
options.why: Nothing in the question says that testing destroys a screen. Even if a test were destructive, that would not mean no sample could be tested.

options.text: All $900$ screens can be assumed to be fault-free because these three passed
options.why: A test of three screens does not establish that the other $897$ screens are fault-free.

questions.solution_text:
Only $3$ of the $900$ screens were tested. Faults among the other $897$ screens may have been missed. A few successful tests do not show that the whole delivery is fault-free.
**Three screens are far too few to show how common a fault is in $900$**.

questions.question_text:
A zoo sells child, adult, concession and family tickets in very different numbers, and wants to know how visitors on each ticket type rate the new walkway.
Which sampling method best suits this aim?

options.text: Stratified sampling, with the four ticket types as the groups
Self-selected sampling, using a feedback box at the walkway exit
options.why: Collects replies only from visitors who chose to write one, missing the rest entirely.

options.text: Simple random sampling from the list of all tickets sold
options.why: Is fair overall but leaves the number from each ticket type to chance, which the comparison needs fixed.

options.text: Systematic sampling, taking every $20$th visitor through the gate
options.why: Spreads the sample across the day but cannot guarantee each ticket type is represented in proportion.

questions.solution_text:
The zoo wants to compare views across ticket types, which are sold in different numbers.
**Use stratified sampling, with ticket type as the groups**. Choose visitors at random within each type. A proportional sample fixes each type’s share in advance instead of leaving those numbers to chance.

questions.question_text:
A university wants to know how its students rate campus parking.
Method $1$ draws $400$ students at random from the full enrolment roll and receives an answer from each of them.
Method $2$ places an open poll on the student website, which collects $6000$ responses.
Which method gives the more reliable estimate, and why?

options.text: Method $1$, because every student had an equal chance of being contacted
Method $2$, because $6000$ responses is a much larger sample than $400$
options.why: Treats a large self-selected sample as reliable simply because it is large.

options.text: Method $2$, because an open poll reaches students who use the website daily
options.why: Reaching students who use the website daily does not establish the views of all students. The open poll still relies on people choosing to reply.

options.text: Method $1$, because $400$ is close to a tenth of the students enrolled
options.why: The total enrolment is not given, so the claim about a tenth cannot be checked. The reason for choosing Method $1$ is its random selection from the full roll.

questions.solution_text:
Method $1$ chooses at random from the full enrolment roll, and all $400$ selected students answer. Every student had an equal chance of selection.
Method $2$ collects voluntary replies from website users. People who do not use the website or choose not to answer are missing, and their views may differ.
**Method $1$, because every student had an equal chance of being contacted**. More replies to the open poll do not remove volunteer bias.

questions.question_text:
A club has an ordered list of $4000$ members and wants a systematic sample of $50$.
Which description of the procedure is correct and complete?

options.text: Choose a random start from members $1$ to $80$, then take every $80$th member
Start at member $1$, then take every $80$th member from there
options.why: Fixes the start instead of randomising it, so the same members are chosen every time.

options.text: Choose a random start from members $1$ to $50$, then take every $50$th member
options.why: Uses the sample size as the step instead of dividing $4000$ by $50$.

options.text: Choose $50$ random numbers from $1$ to $4000$ and take those members
options.why: Describes a simple random sample, which uses no fixed step through the list.

questions.solution_text:
$k=\frac{4000}{50}$
$=80$
The start must be chosen at random from the first $80$ members, otherwise the sample is fixed by the list order alone.
**Choose a random start from members $1$ to $80$, then take every $80$th member**.
